title: Group Anagrams
description:
Given an array of strings `strs`, group all **anagrams** together. You may return the groups in **any order**, and the strings within each group may also be in **any order**.

An **anagram** is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, using all the original letters exactly once. Duplicate strings are anagrams of each other and must each appear in the resulting group with their original multiplicity.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Two strings are anagrams if and only if they have the exact same character frequencies (or identical sorted character sequences).
Use a canonical signature for each string as the key in a hash map whose value is the list of strings sharing that signature.
Using a 26-element letter count tuple/key avoids sorting each string and achieves O(n * k) time where k is the maximum string length.

examples.explanation: "eat", "tea", and "ate" share the letter counts {a:1, e:1, t:1}; "tan" and "nat" share {a:1, n:1, t:1}; "bat" forms its own group.
A single empty string forms a single group containing [""].
A single-character string forms a single group [["a"]].

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description:
Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the **longest consecutive elements sequence** (i.e., values `x, x + 1, x + 2, ..., x + k - 1` that all appear somewhere in `nums`).

Duplicate values do not extend the length of a consecutive sequence, and elements do not need to be adjacent in `nums`. If `nums` is empty, return `0`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(n)` average time.
hints: Putting all numbers into a hash set gives O(1) average lookup and automatically eliminates duplicates.
Only start counting a sequence from a value x when x - 1 is NOT in the set, so x is guaranteed to be the start of a maximal run.
Iterate over the unique elements in the set (not the original array) so duplicate starts cannot cause repeated work; each element is visited at most twice overall.

examples.explanation: The longest consecutive elements sequence is [1, 2, 3, 4], which has length 4.
The sequence [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] has length 9; duplicate 0 does not add to the length.
An empty array contains no consecutive sequence, so return 0.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
description:
Implement the `RandomizedSet` class supporting insert, remove, and uniform random retrieval in **average `O(1)` time**:

- `RandomizedSet()` initializes an empty `RandomizedSet` object.
- `bool insert(int val)` inserts `val` into the set if not present. Returns `true` if the item was not present, `false` otherwise.
- `bool remove(int val)` removes `val` from the set if present. Returns `true` if the item was present, `false` otherwise.
- `int getRandom()` returns a random element from the current set of elements (it is guaranteed that at least one element exists when this method is called). Each element must have the **same probability** of being returned.

Because `getRandom()` is randomized, the judge validates every operation return value and verifies that every `getRandom()` returns a valid member of the set with non-degenerate randomness, returning `true` when all checks pass.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls will be made to insert, remove, and getRandom.
There will be at least one element in the data structure when getRandom is called.
hints: A hash set supports O(1) insert and remove, but cannot pick a uniformly random element in O(1) time; a dynamic array supports O(1) random indexing, but removing from the middle takes O(n).
Combine both: store values in a dynamic array and maintain a hash map from value to its current index in the array.
To remove a value in O(1), overwrite its slot in the array with the last element, update the last element's index in the hash map, and pop the array's tail.

examples.explanation: insert(1)->true, remove(2)->false, insert(2)->true, getRandom()->1 or 2, remove(1)->true, insert(2)->false, getRandom()->2. All operations pass validation.
Removing the only element and re-inserting it keeps the internal array and index map consistent.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
description:
`RandomizedCollection` is a data structure that contains a collection of numbers, possibly **duplicates** (i.e., a multiset). It must support inserting and removing specific elements and retrieving a random element in **average `O(1)` time**:

- `RandomizedCollection()` initializes an empty `RandomizedCollection` object.
- `bool insert(int val)` inserts one copy of `val` into the multiset, even if `val` is already present. Returns `true` if `val` was **not** present before this insertion, and `false` otherwise.
- `bool remove(int val)` removes **one** copy of `val` from the multiset if present. Returns `true` if `val` was present, and `false` otherwise. If `val` has multiple occurrences, only one copy is removed.
- `int getRandom()` returns a random element from the current multiset of elements. The probability of each distinct value being returned is **linearly proportional** to the number of copies of that value currently in the multiset.

Because `getRandom()` is randomized, the judge validates every `insert`/`remove` return value, checks every `getRandom()` is currently in the multiset, and verifies non-degenerate weighted randomness, returning `true` when all checks pass.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls in total will be made to insert, remove, and getRandom.
There will be at least one element in the data structure when getRandom is called.
hints: Extend the array + hash map pattern from RandomizedSet by mapping each value to a set of all indices where it currently resides in the array.
On remove(val), pop any index idx from pos[val]. If idx is not the last index in the array, move the last element into idx and update its index set by removing lastIdx and adding idx.
Be careful when val equals the last element in the array: remove idx from pos[val] first, and only update pos[lastVal] if idx != lastIdx.

examples.explanation: insert(1)->true, insert(1)->false (now [1,1]), insert(2)->true (now [1,1,2]), getRandom()->1 (2/3 prob) or 2 (1/3 prob), remove(1)->true (now [1,2]), getRandom()->1 or 2 equally.
Removing all copies of a value makes the next remove return false and the next insert return true.

title: Isomorphic Strings
description:
Given two strings `s` and `t` of equal length, determine if they are **isomorphic**.

Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`. All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. No two distinct characters may map to the same character, though a character may map to itself.

Return `true` if `s` and `t` are isomorphic, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII characters.
hints: Checking only a one-way map from s to t is not enough: two distinct characters in s could wrongly map to the same character in t.
Maintain two maps (s -> t and t -> s) to enforce a strict one-to-one bijection between characters.
Alternatively, track the last seen 1-based position of each ASCII character in two fixed arrays of size 256; at each index i, both characters must have identical last-seen positions.

examples.explanation: 'e' maps to 'a' and 'g' maps to 'd', forming a valid bijection.
'o' would need to map to both 'a' and 'r', which is invalid.
'p'->'t', 'a'->'i', 'e'->'l', 'r'->'e' is a valid one-to-one mapping.

title: Word Pattern
description:
Given a `pattern` and a string `s`, determine if `s` follows the exact same pattern.

Here **follow** means a full match such that there is a **bijection** between each letter in `pattern` and each non-empty space-separated word in `s`:
- Each letter in `pattern` maps to exactly one unique word in `s`.
- Each unique word in `s` maps to exactly one letter in `pattern`.
- The number of characters in `pattern` must equal the number of words in `s`.

Return `true` if `s` follows `pattern`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: pattern contains only lowercase English letters.
s contains only lowercase English letters and spaces ' '.
s does not contain any leading or trailing spaces.
All the words in s are separated by a single space.
hints: First split s on single spaces and immediately return false if the number of words does not equal len(pattern).
Maintain two hash maps: char_to_word and word_to_char so neither two letters map to the same word nor one letter maps to two different words.
Avoid merging characters and words into a single unprefixed map, because single-letter words like 'a' can collide with pattern letters.

examples.explanation: 'a' <-> "dog" and 'b' <-> "cat" form a valid bijection.
'a' maps to "dog" at index 0, so it cannot map to "fish" at index 3.
'a' maps to "dog" and 'b' also tries to map to "dog", violating the bijection.

title: First Unique Character in a String
description: Given a string `s`, find the **first non-repeating character** in it and return its 0-based index. If no character appears exactly once, return `-1`.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.
hints: Count the total frequency of each of the 26 lowercase English letters in a first pass over the string.
In a second pass from left to right, return the first index whose character has a total frequency of 1.
Because the alphabet size is fixed at 26, a length-26 integer array uses O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: 'l' at index 0 is the first character that does not repeat anywhere in the string.
'l', 'o', and 'e' all repeat; 'v' at index 2 is the first unique character.
Every character ('a' and 'b') appears twice, so return -1.

title: Design HashMap
description:
Design a HashMap **without using any built-in hash table libraries**.

Implement the `MyHashMap` class:
- `MyHashMap()` initializes the object with an empty map.
- `void put(int key, int value)` inserts a `(key, value)` pair into the HashMap. If the `key` already exists in the map, update the corresponding `value`.
- `int get(int key)` returns the `value` to which the specified `key` is mapped, or `-1` if this map contains no mapping for the `key`.
- `void remove(int key)` removes the `key` and its corresponding `value` if the map contains a mapping for the `key`.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls will be made to put, get, and remove.
hints: Allocate a fixed array of buckets whose length is a prime number (such as 2069) to minimize clustering.
Map each key to a bucket via key % numBuckets, and resolve collisions inside each bucket using separate chaining (a linked list or small list of (key, value) pairs).
Remember that 0 is a valid stored value, so only return -1 when the key is genuinely absent from its bucket.

examples.explanation: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1)->1, get(3)->-1, put(2,1) updates key 2, get(2)->1, remove(2), get(2)->-1.
Storing value 0 at key 0 must return 0 (not -1), and removing a missing key is a no-op.

title: Design Twitter
description:
Design a simplified version of Twitter where users can post tweets, follow/unfollow other users, and retrieve the `10` most recent tweets in their news feed.

Implement the `Twitter` class:
- `Twitter()` initializes your Twitter object.
- `void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId)` composes a new tweet with ID `tweetId` by user `userId`. Each call to this function will be made with a unique `tweetId`.
- `List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId)` retrieves the `10` most recent tweet IDs in the user's news feed. Each item in the news feed must be posted by users whom `userId` followed or by `userId` themself. Tweets must be ordered from **most recent to least recent**.
- `void follow(int followerId, int followeeId)` the user with ID `followerId` starts following the user with ID `followeeId`.
- `void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId)` the user with ID `followerId` stops following the user with ID `followeeId`.

Following a user who is already followed or unfollowing a user who is not currently followed has no effect. When a user follows someone, that followee's previously posted tweets immediately become eligible for the follower's news feed.
constraints: All tweets have unique tweetId values.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to postTweet, getNewsFeed, follow, and unfollow.
followerId != followeeId for all follow and unfollow calls.
hints: Assign a monotonically increasing integer timestamp to every posted tweet so recency can be compared in O(1).
Store each user's tweets in a per-user list (already sorted by timestamp) and each user's followees in a hash set.
To build getNewsFeed(userId), run a k-way merge with a max-heap over the tail of the tweet lists belonging to userId and their followees, popping at most 10 tweets.
timeComplexity: O(1) post/follow/unfollow, O(k log k) getNewsFeed

examples.explanation: User 1 posts 5 -> feed [5]; follows 2 who posts 6 -> feed [6, 5]; unfollows 2 -> feed [5].
A user with no tweets and no followees gets an empty feed; following someone retrospectively includes their earlier tweets.

title: Analyze User Website Visit Pattern
description:
You are given two string arrays `username` and `website` and an integer array `timestamp`, all of the same length `n`. The tuple `[username[i], timestamp[i], website[i]]` indicates that user `username[i]` visited website `website[i]` at time `timestamp[i]`.

A **pattern** is a list of **three** websites (not necessarily distinct). A user visits a pattern `(w1, w2, w3)` if they visited `w1`, then later `w2`, and then later `w3` in strictly increasing timestamp order (not necessarily consecutively).

The **score** of a pattern is the number of **distinct users** who visited all the websites in the pattern in that chronological order. (If the same user matches a pattern multiple times, that user still contributes only `1` to that pattern's score.)

Return the pattern with the **largest score**. If multiple patterns tie for the largest score, return the **lexicographically smallest** pattern (comparing element 0, then element 1, then element 2 using standard string ordering).
constraints: username[i] and website[i] consist of lowercase English letters.
It is guaranteed that there is at least one user who visited at least three websites.
No user visits two websites at the same timestamp.
hints: Input records are not guaranteed to be sorted by timestamp — group visits by username and sort each user's visits by timestamp ascending.
For each user, enumerate all 3-website combinations (i < j < k) and store them in a per-user set so each user increments a pattern's score at most once.
Track the pattern with the maximum count, breaking ties by comparing the 3-tuple of website strings lexicographically.

examples.explanation: joe visited [home, about, career], james visited [home, cart, maps, home], mary visited [home, about, career]. Pattern [home, about, career] has score 2 (joe and mary).
ua visited [a, b, a] and ub visited [a, b, c]. Both patterns have score 1, and [a, b, a] is lexicographically smaller than [a, b, c].
